newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish tax debate at a glance - possible scenarios.
newsitem.headline: Polish tax debate at a glance - possible scenarios.

text.p: The Polish Senate votes this week on tax bills which will determine the shape of the 1997 budget.

The government, which has submitted a budget draft based on this year's tax levels and assuming a deficit at 2.6 percent of gross domestic product, last month offered a moderate tax cut which would keep the deficit unchanged from this year's planned 2.8 percent of GDP.
But the government proposals were rejected in an October 24 vote by the lower house of parliament, the Sejm.
The ruling coalition's Peasant Party (PSL) voted with the opposition to defeat its larger partner, the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), the only party to back the government scheme.
The Sejm instead passed a four-level tax scale sharply cutting taxes for the lowest paid, despite government protests that this would increase the deficit and raise inflation.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski has signalled that he supports the government scheme and will veto the tax bill if the Senate passes the lower house's proposed tax levels.
Since then, Peasant Party senators and senate committees have proposed alternative tax levels. The outcome will depend on how the Peasant Party and opposition vote.
Here is a summary of some tax proposals and their impact on the 1997 budget, as estimated by the Finance Ministry.
TAX RATES (pct) 1997 BUDGET
change in revenues deficit
bln PLN pct GDP
Sejm bill 17, 20, 33, 45 -3.6 3.0 plus
Government 20, 31, 43 -2.0 2.8
PSL senators 18, 20, 33, 44 n.a. n.a.
Senate committees 20, 32, 44 n.a. n.a.
SOME POSSIBLE SCENARIOS

* The Senate passes the lower house's tax rates. The bill goes to President Kwasniewski, who has 20 days to sign it into law or veto it. If he applies the veto as he has suggested, the bill goes back to the Sejm, which needs a two-thirds majority to overrule the veto. The SLD has 167 out of 460 seats, more than the one-third needed to uphold the veto. It does so.
OUTCOME - Tax rates remain unchanged, as parliament cannot pass another bill before the November 30 deadline for tax changes. Budget deficit of 2.6 percent of GDP in 1997.
According to Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz the government will propose a limited amendment to the current tax law to eliminate some tax breaks and loopholes.

* The Senate amends the tax bill to fit government proposals. The lower house votes next week, the Peasants or the opposition relent and the bill passes, going to the President who immediately signs it so that the bill takes effect before the November 30 deadline.
OUTCOME - Lower taxes, deficit at 2.8 percent of GDP.

* The Senate amends the tax bill to conform with the government plan but the lower house finds a sufficient majority (more than 50 percent of those voting) to reject the changes. The original Sejm bill goes to the President, who vetoes it.
OUTCOME - Tax rates unchanged, deficit at 2.6 percent.
* The Senate amends the tax bill according to a moderated PSL proposal, the SLD fails to garner a sufficient majority to reject it, but Kwasniewski vetoes the bill.
OUTCOME - Tax rates unchanged, deficit at 2.6 percent.
* The Senate amends the tax bill acccording to the altered PSL proposal, the lower house rejects it, the Sejm bill remains intact, which Kwasniewski vetoes.
OUTCOME - Taxes rates unchanged, deficit at 2.6 percent.

* The ruling coalition strikes a last-minute compromise, which envisages a deeper tax cut than the government proposal but less radical than the Sejm's, the bill clears the Senate and the lower house, President Kwasniewski signs it into law.
OUTCOME - Taxes lowered on a yet undetermined scale, budget deficit probably in the 2.8-3.0 percent range.
